title: Calling the weapons back
hook: a young man with the gods' weapons asks the one question that matters next
carry: the wise know samhara, the calling back

segments.voice: Yesterday: divine powers stood before Rama as shining beings, and he asked them to stay in his mind. Your line was the guru gives mantras to the ready.
screen: `THE GURU GIVES MANTRAS TO THE READY.`

segments.voice: Hand someone the keys to something enormous and listen to their first question. A new driver with a fast car. A new manager with the power to fire people. An eighteen-year-old with a credit card. It's nearly always: what can this do? How fast, how far, how much? Rama has just been handed the weapons of the gods. And walking on through the forest, he asks Vishvamitra something quieter, and wiser.
screen: `THE KEYS TO SOMETHING ENORMOUS.` → `THE USUAL QUESTION: WHAT CAN IT DO?` → `RAMA ASKS ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: I've received the weapons, Rama says, and even the gods would find them hard to overcome. Now teach me how to call them back. In Sanskrit, the release is prayoga; the withdrawal is samhara. Vishvamitra is delighted, and teaches him. Again the powers appear, a new company of shining beings, palms joined. These are the withdrawals: the knowledge of how to stop what you've started. Why does Valmiki give this a whole moment? Because in the epics a weapon you can't call back is a disaster. Rama, this young, asks for the brake before he ever touches the accelerator. And the same word comes back in the Bhagavad Gita. Krishna describes a person of steady wisdom as someone who can draw the senses back from what pulls at them, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs: yada samharate, when he withdraws. Samhara, again. That's a Hindu idea of strength. Not only what you can unleash, but what you can call back: a word, an appetite, a temper. The road goes on to a green hermitage on a hill, with deer grazing. This is Siddhashrama, the sage says, where Vishnu once did his austerities, the hermitage of Vamana, who asked King Bali for three steps of land and crossed the worlds in three strides. My sacrifice is waiting here. And here the weapons will be needed.
screen: `TEACH ME TO CALL THEM BACK.` · `PRAYOGA AND SAMHARA.` · `THE GITA: YADĀ SAṂHARATE CĀYAṂ KŪRMO 'ṄGĀNĪVA SARVAŚAḤ.` · `SIDDHASHRAMA, WHERE VAMANA LIVED.` · then, large: `SAṂHĀRA: THE WITHDRAWAL.`

segments.voice: Sit like the Gita's tortoise. Let attention come in from the world one sense at a time: the eyes soften, then the ears, then the busy hands go still. Every breath has a release and a return. Then think of one thing you set loose today, a mood, a comment, a scroll that ran too long, and practice calling it back, the way a breath comes home. If you pray, ask for that kind of strength.
The weapons. Rama asks not only how to release them but how to withdraw them, and Vishvamitra teaches him the samhara, the calling back.
Your line: the wise know samhara, the calling back. Rama asked for the brake first. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Traditional teachers often point to Rama's request for the withdrawals of the weapons as a sign of his character, and the Gita's image of the tortoise drawing in its limbs uses the same word for self-mastery.

what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 28 gives the samhara mantras, also embodied as beings; sarga 29 names Siddhashrama as the place of Vishnu's tapas and the hermitage of Vamana. Gita 2.58 uses saṃharate for the sage who draws in the senses like a tortoise.
